title: A/B Test Sample Sizing
intro: There is no standard A/B sample size. “We always test with 200” skips every input that makes the number meaningful.

learn.title: Four inputs
learn.text:
**Baseline** — what happens today, e.g. 18% complete the task
**MDE** — the minimum detectable effect: the smallest improvement worth shipping
**Confidence** — 90% or 95%, agreed up front
**Power** — the chance of detecting a real effect, typically 80%

Change any one of these and the required number changes.

try.q: Which input is a business judgement rather than a statistical setting?
try.explain: How much better B must be to be worth shipping is a product decision.

learn.title: Calabro's example
learn.text:
18% of users complete the task today. Moving to 19% wouldn't justify a redesign; the team agrees that **about 26%** would.

That 8-point improvement is the MDE — and it came from a conversation with the product team, not from a calculator.

So stakeholders belong in the sample-size discussion, which is not where most teams put them.

try.q: Where did the 8-point MDE in his example come from?
options: A conversation with the product team
Industry benchmarks for the same sector
try.explain: “How much better must B be for this to be worth shipping?”

right.label: A sized test
items: Confidence and power set up front

learn.title: Sizing in practice
learn.text:
Take the **baseline from analytics** if you have it; a reasoned estimate beats ignoring it.

Set **confidence and power** from your organisation's agreed standard rather than per-test.

Then explain the final number to stakeholders in terms of the decision: this many users, to be able to tell an 8-point improvement from noise.

Halving the MDE roughly quadruples the sample — which is why chasing one-point lifts on low-traffic flows rarely works.

try.q: You halve the MDE. Roughly what happens to the required sample?
try.explain: Which is why small lifts need very large samples.

test.q: Why is there no standard A/B sample size?
options: Traffic varies too much between products
test.explain: Four inputs, each of which moves the number. Confidence and power.

options: The chance of detecting a real effect
The size of the difference you observed

test.q: What should you do if you have no baseline data?
options: Run the test until it reaches significance
test.explain: A reasoned estimate beats ignoring the input.

test.q: How should the final number be explained to stakeholders?
options: In terms of the decision it supports
Relative to the last test the team ran
test.explain: This many users, to tell that size of improvement from noise.

test.q: Why are one-point lifts on low-traffic flows a problem?
options: They are almost never worth shipping
test.explain: Halving the MDE roughly quadruples the sample.
